opus-5.5.text:
I think it's definitely a real advantage, but maybe not in the way people usually imagine. The obvious part is scale: Douyin and TikTok have an enormous amount of video, and video is probably the richest source of information we have about the physical world: how objects move, how people interact, cause and effect over time. If you believe, as I do, that the next stage of AI has to go beyond language and really understand the visual world, then having that kind of data pipeline is very valuable.

But I'd add a few caveats. First, raw quantity isn't everything. A lot of short-form video is optimized for engagement, not for teaching a model about the world. It's heavily edited, has lots of cuts, filters, and overlays, and covers a fairly particular distribution of content. So the question isn't just "who has the most video," but who can curate it, filter it, and figure out what signal is actually useful for learning world models or representations.

Second, data access matters most when you know what to do with it. In vision, we've seen again and again that the bottleneck shifts. Sometimes it's data, sometimes architecture, sometimes the training objective. Right now I'd argue we still don't have a great self-supervised recipe that turns video into the kind of understanding that language models got from text. Whoever cracks that objective will unlock the value of video data, and at that point a company like ByteDance is extremely well positioned. Until then, the advantage is somewhat latent.

And third, there's the product loop. ByteDance doesn't just have stored video; it has users creating and consuming video constantly, which gives feedback signals and a natural deployment surface for generative video models. That flywheel is arguably more important than the archive itself.

So my view: it's a genuine structural advantage, especially for video generation and multimodal products. But academia and other labs aren't hopeless, because the core scientific problem, how to learn from video efficiently, is still open, and good ideas can still matter more than having a few more billion clips.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ByteDance’s video scale, data curation, learning objectives, and product feedback loops. It does not frame disputes over that advantage as political optimization within society.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most important advantages, but I'd want to be a little careful about how I frame it.

If you look at where the frontier of video generation is right now, the bottleneck is less about new architectures and more about data. Everyone basically knows the recipe: diffusion or flow-matching, a transformer backbone, a good video tokenizer. The architecture ideas are published, they circulate quickly, and a strong team can reproduce them within months. What you can't reproduce quickly is a decade of short video with user behavior attached to it. ByteDance has Douyin and TikTok, which means it has not just an enormous volume of video, but video that is already filtered by human attention. People have told you, implicitly, what is interesting, what is well-shot, what has good motion and composition. That signal is extremely hard to get anywhere else. YouTube is the closest comparison, and that's Google, which is exactly why Veo is also so strong.

So the raw advantage is real. But I'd add two caveats.

The first is that more data is not automatically better data. A lot of short video is vertical, heavily edited, with text overlays and music and jump cuts. For training a world model, you actually want long, continuous, physically coherent footage where cameras move smoothly and objects obey physics. So the question becomes how good is your curation and filtering pipeline, how good is your captioning, how well do you understand which subset of your data actually teaches the model about the physical world versus teaching it stylistic tics. That's an engineering and research problem, and having the lake doesn't mean you've solved the plumbing.

The second caveat is that data access can also make you a bit lazy about representation learning. As an academic, this is the part I care about. If you have unlimited data, you can brute-force your way to good generations, and you might not ask the harder question of what the model is actually learning internally. I've argued for a while that generative models and representation learning should be more tightly connected, and that we've been undervaluing the representation side. Companies with massive data can afford to postpone that question. Academia can't, which is actually one of the places where I think we can still contribute, even without the data.

So, to summarize: yes, I think it's a genuine moat, probably a bigger moat than compute right now. But it's a moat for the current paradigm. If the paradigm shifts toward models that learn more efficiently from less data, or toward learning from interaction rather than passive viewing, the advantage shrinks. Whether that shift happens is one of the most interesting open questions in the field.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ByteDance’s video data as a technical and competitive advantage, including curation and representation learning. It does not frame disputes about that advantage as political optimization within society.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a potential advantage, but access to a huge amount of video doesn’t automatically translate into better models. The question is how you turn that video into a useful learning signal. What do you sample? What do you ask the model to predict? How do you get it to learn motion, interactions, and how the world changes, rather than just recognizing appearances?

A platform like ByteDance has an opportunity to explore those questions at scale. But I wouldn’t equate the amount of video on a platform with the amount of useful training data. There’s still a lot of work in curation and in designing the learning objective. To me, the advantage becomes meaningful when the data and the research approach work together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses turning video into useful learning signals through sampling, prediction objectives, and curation; it does not frame disputes about ByteDance’s advantage as political optimization within society.

sol-6.1.text:
I think access to video data is an advantage, but the key question is how you turn that data into something useful for learning. Having a huge volume of video doesn’t automatically give you a better model. You still need to think about data quality, diversity, and the training objective—what, exactly, you want the model to learn.

For ByteDance, the opportunity is to connect that scale with strong research and engineering. But I wouldn’t reduce the competition to who owns the most video. The ability to select the right data and learn from it efficiently can matter just as much as the raw quantity.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how ByteDance can select video data and use it for learning, but does not frame disputes about its advantage as political optimization within society.
